teaching.causalExplanation: It's the flask. Concentration isn't how much solute there is altogether. It's how much is packed into each part of the solution. Take the same small sample, one millilitre, from each. The flask's millilitre holds twice as many calcium chloride units as the beaker's. So the beaker has more solute in total, but the flask is more concentrated. A quick reminder of the words. The solute is what dissolves, the solvent is the water it dissolves in, and the solution is the mixture. In chemistry, we measure concentration as the number of moles of solute in each litre of solution. So the formula is c equals n over V. The concentration in moles per litre equals the chemical amount in moles, divided by the volume of the solution in litres. The unit tells you the formula. Moles per litre means moles divided by litres. You'll also see moles per litre written as a capital M, short for molar. Lab volumes are usually in millilitres, so convert first. There are a thousand millilitres in a litre, so divide by a thousand. Fifty millilitres is zero point zero five zero zero litres. So our flask is zero point zero two zero zero moles over zero point zero five zero zero litres, which is zero point four zero zero moles per litre. The beaker is zero point one zero zero over zero point five zero zero, which is zero point two zero zero. The flask is twice as concentrated, just like the picture. Put in fifty instead of zero point zero five, and your answer comes out a thousand times too small.
